claim: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) is richly endowed with both opioid peptides and their respective receptors.
source: One candidate neural substrate is the brain's opioid system, particularly in the ventral striatum. A role for this circuitry is supported by observations that the ventral striatum, and in particular the nucleus accumbens (NAc), is richly endowed with both opioid peptides and their respective receptors (Mansour et al., 1988)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mansour et al., 1988

claim: Activation of NAc µ-opioid receptors (MORs) selectively augments consumption of palatable food.
source: activation of NAc µ-opioid receptors (MORs) selectively augments consumption of palatable food (Bakshi and Kelley, 1993; Mucha and Iversen, 1986; Zhang et al., 1998; Zhang and Kelley, 1997)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Activation of NAc MORs increases consumption of preferred flavors.
source: activation of NAc µ-opioid receptors (MORs) selectively augments consumption of palatable food (Bakshi and Kelley, 1993; Mucha and Iversen, 1986; Zhang et al., 1998; Zhang and Kelley, 1997) and of preferred flavors (Woolley et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Woolley et al., 2006

claim: Activation of NAc MORs increases hedonic taste reactions to palatable food.
source: Moreover, activation of NAc MORs increases hedonic taste reactions to palatable food (Peciña and Berridge, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Peciña and Berridge, 2000

claim: Blockade of NAc MORs does not consistently reduce calorie-dense food consumption.
source: First, blockade of NAc MORs does not consistently reduce calorie-dense food consumption (Bodnar et al., 1995; Kelley et al., 1996; Lardeux et al., 2015; MacDonald et al., 2003; Ward et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Activation of NAc MORs increases breaking point on a progressive-ratio task.
source: In addition, activation of NAc MORs increases certain measures of reward-seeking behavior, including breaking point on a progressive-ratio task (Zhang et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2003

claim: Activation of NAc MORs increases lever pressing in the presence of food-predictive cues in a Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer task.
source: activation of NAc MORs increases certain measures of reward-seeking behavior, including breaking point on a progressive-ratio task (Zhang et al., 2003) and lever pressing in the presence of food-predictive cues in a Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer task (Peciña and Berridge, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Peciña and Berridge, 2013

claim: NAc neurons encode both cued approach and reward consumption phases of behaviors.
source: NAc neurons encode both cued approach and reward consumption phases of such behaviors (Ambroggi et al., 2011; du Hoffmann and Nicola, 2014; McGinty et al., 2013; Morrison et al., 2017; Nicola, 2010; Nicola et al., 2004a; 2004b; Taha and Fields, 2005)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Cue-evoked excitations in NAc neurons are necessary for the approach response.
source: cue-evoked excitations are necessary for the approach response (Ambroggi et al., 2008; du Hoffmann and Nicola, 2014; Yun et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Bilateral CTAP injection into the NAc reduced CS+ response ratio in free-fed rats.
source: Bilateral CTAP (4 µg/side) injection into the NAc reduced CS+ response ratio in free-fed (solid lines), but not food-restricted rats (dashed lines). A two-factor ANOVA (time x dose) performed on free-fed rats revealed significant main effects of dose (F2,180 = 12.28, p<0.001) and time (F3,180 = 12.28, p<0.001)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1C

claim: CTAP had no effect on CS+ responding in food-restricted rats.
source: Bilateral CTAP (4 µg/side) injection into the NAc reduced CS+ response ratio in free-fed (solid lines), but not food-restricted rats (dashed lines)... ANOVA revealed no significant effects in food-restricted rats (dose, F2,64 = 2.27, p=0.11; time, F3,64 = 2.11, p=0.11; dose x time F6,64 = 1.16, p=0.34)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1C

claim: CTAP had no effect on CS+ responding for 3% sucrose reward in free-fed rats.
source: When the reward was 3% sucrose instead of heavy cream, CTAP had no effect on CS+ responding in free-fed rats (N = 8). A two-factor ANOVA revealed a main effect of time (F3,84 = 13.54, p<0.001), but not dose (F2,84 = 0.51, p=0.605). The time x dose interaction was not significant (F6,84 = 0.70, p=0.66)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1D

claim: Food-restricted rats responded to a significantly higher proportion of cues than free-fed rats.
source: By the final day of retraining, food-restricted rats responded to a significantly higher proportion of cues than free-fed rats (Figure 1B, see figure legend for statistics)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: 54.2% of neurons recorded in free-fed rats were excited by the CS+.
source: Out of 83 neurons recorded in 12 free-fed rats, 45 neurons were excited by the CS+ (54.2%; Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 74.5% of neurons recorded in food-restricted rats were excited by the CS+.
source: as opposed to 91 out of 122 neurons (74.5%; Figure 2B) recorded from five food-restricted rats
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The magnitude of the cue-excited population response in food-restricted rats was significantly greater than the response in free-fed rats.
source: Further, the magnitude of the cue-excited population response in food-restricted rats was significantly greater than the response in free-fed rats (Figure 2C,D)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data and statistical comparison shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: The fraction of 50 ms time bins after cue onset with significant excitations was greater in food-restricted rats than in free-fed rats.
source: as was the fraction of 50 ms time bins after cue onset with significant excitations (Figure 2E,F, upper traces/dots)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2E,F

claim: The average speed of approach after cue onset was significantly greater in restricted rats than in free-fed rats.
source: We found that the average speed of approach after cue onset was significantly greater in restricted rats, while latency to maximum speed and distance did not differ (Figure 2G)
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Lower cue-evoked excitation in free-fed than in restricted rats is not wholly accounted for by lower response vigor.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that lower cue-evoked excitation in free-fed than in restricted rats is not wholly accounted for by lower response vigor, which suggests that additional, unaccounted factors push firing rate lower in free-fed animals than their lower response vigor would predict (or, equivalently, higher in restricted animals than their greater vigor would predict)
evidence: Supported by GLM analysis comparing actual and modeled spike counts shown in Figure 2H

claim: 37.3% of neurons in free-fed rats were excited during reward consumption.
source: In free-fed rats, 37.3% (31 out of 83) of neurons were excited for at least a single 400 ms bin following entry into the receptacle on rewarded trials
evidence: Supported by neural recording data during reward consumption

claim: 60.7% of neurons in food-restricted rats were excited during reward consumption.
source: compared to 60.7% (74 out 122) of neurons in food-restricted rats
evidence: Supported by neural recording data during reward consumption

claim: More bins exhibited significant excitation during reward consumption in restricted than free-fed rats.
source: moreover, more bins exhibited significant excitation in restricted than free-fed rats (Figure 3D, upper dots)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 3D

claim: 32.5% of neurons in free-fed rats were inhibited during reward consumption.
source: There was also a prominent population of reward-associated inhibitions in each group: 32.5% (27 out of 83) were inhibited for at least one bin following rewarded receptacle entry in free-fed rats
evidence: Supported by neural recording data during reward consumption

claim: 34.4% of neurons in food-restricted rats were inhibited during reward consumption.
source: compared to 34.4% (42 out of 122) in food-restricted rats
evidence: Supported by neural recording data during reward consumption

claim: There was no difference in the fraction of bins with significant inhibition during reward consumption between free-fed and food-restricted rats.
source: Unlike excitations, there was no difference in the fraction of bins with significant inhibition between the two groups (Figure 3D, lower dots)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 3D

claim: CTAP sharply attenuated responding to the CS+ in bilaterally-injected free-fed rats.
source: As we previously observed (Figure 1C), in bilaterally-injected free-fed rats, CTAP sharply attenuated responding to the CS+ (Figure 4A,B blue trace and bars)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: CTAP had no effect on CS+ responding in bilaterally-injected food-restricted rats.
source: while the drug had no effect in food-restricted rats (Figure 4A,B red trace and bars)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: Cue-evoked excitations in NAc neurons were significantly attenuated following CTAP injection in free-fed rats.
source: During the behavior shown in Figure 4, cue-evoked excitations in NAc neurons were significantly attenuated following CTAP injection in free-fed rats (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: The magnitude of cue-evoked excitations in food-restricted animals was unchanged by CTAP.
source: In contrast, the magnitude of cue-evoked excitations in food-restricted animals was unchanged (Figure 5C,D,G,H)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 5C,D,G,H

claim: The fraction of significantly excited bins was reduced by CTAP in free-fed rats.
source: This was true of both the magnitude of the excitations (Figure 5E,F) and the fraction of significantly excited bins (Figure 5J)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 5J

claim: The fraction of significantly excited bins was unchanged by CTAP in food-restricted rats.
source: as was the fraction of significantly excited bins (Figure 5L)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 5L

claim: CTAP injection had no effect on baseline firing rate in free-fed rats.
source: However, CTAP injection had no effect on baseline firing rate in free-fed rats, as the slope of the regression line of pre- vs. post- baseline firing rate did not significantly differ from the unity line (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by analysis of baseline firing rates shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: Neurons ipsilateral to unilateral CTAP injection exhibited a significant reduction in the magnitude of cue-evoked excitations post-injection.
source: In neurons ipsilateral to the CTAP injection (i.e., neurons directly exposed to drug), we observed a significant reduction in the magnitude of cue-evoked excitations post-injection (Figure 6A,B,E,F)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 6A,B,E,F

claim: Neurons contralateral to unilateral CTAP injection exhibited no significant reduction in the magnitude of cue-evoked excitations.
source: In contrast, neurons contralateral to the injection (i.e., not exposed to drug; Figure 6C,D) exhibited no significant reduction in the magnitude of cue-evoked excitations (Figure 6G,H)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 6G,H

claim: The proportion of bins with significant excitation or inhibition was significantly decreased for neurons ipsilateral to unilateral CTAP injection.
source: Additionally, among neurons that were classified as cue-excited or cue-inhibited, the proportion of bins with significant excitation or inhibition was significantly decreased for neurons ipsilateral to the injection (Figure 6I,J)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 6I,J

claim: The proportion of bins with significant excitation or inhibition was not significantly decreased for neurons contralateral to unilateral CTAP injection.
source: but not for contralateral neurons (Figure 6K,L)
evidence: Supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 6K,L

claim: Saline injection had no effect on cue-evoked neural activity.
source: Finally, saline injection had no effect on cue-evoked neural activity (Figure 7), demonstrating that the observed change in firing or behavior following CTAP injection cannot be attributed to any physical perturbation by the injection itself
evidence: Supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 7

claim: Consumption-associated firing on a given trial did not significantly predict the probability of a behavioral response on the next trial.
source: For both the consumption-excited and consumption-inhibited population, the spike count on a given trial did not significantly contribute to response probability (p=0.18 and p=0.20, respectively, Wald test)
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis

claim: Unilateral CTAP injection did not significantly affect the total time spent in the receptacle during reward consumption.
source: Finally, unilateral CTAP injection did not significantly affect either the total time spent in the receptacle during reward consumption or the overall number of receptacle entries during the consumption epoch (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Unilateral CTAP injection did not significantly affect the overall number of receptacle entries during the consumption epoch.
source: Finally, unilateral CTAP injection did not significantly affect either the total time spent in the receptacle during reward consumption or the overall number of receptacle entries during the consumption epoch (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Blockade of NAc MORs attenuates both cue-evoked approach to high-fat food and the encoding of those cues by NAc neurons in ad libitum fed rats.
source: We find that blockade of MORs in the NAc core attenuates both cue-evoked approach to high-fat food and the encoding of those cues by NAc neurons, and that these effects are observed only in rats fed ad libitum chow, and not in food-restricted (relatively hungry) rats
evidence: Supported by experimental results from behavioral and neural recording experiments

claim: The effects of NAc MOR blockade on cue-evoked approach and neural encoding are observed only in ad libitum fed rats, not in food-restricted rats.
source: We find that blockade of MORs in the NAc core attenuates both cue-evoked approach to high-fat food and the encoding of those cues by NAc neurons, and that these effects are observed only in rats fed ad libitum chow, and not in food-restricted (relatively hungry) rats
evidence: Supported by experimental results comparing free-fed and food-restricted rats

claim: NAc cue-evoked excitations are causal to cued approach behavior.
source: Notably, NAc cue-evoked excitations are causal to cued approach (du Hoffmann and Nicola, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to du Hoffmann and Nicola, 2014

claim: Activation of NAc MORs by exogenous ligands increases consumption of palatable food when injected into either the NAc core or shell.
source: On the other hand, injection of MOR agonists into either the NAc core or shell increases consumption of palatable food (Bakshi and Kelley, 1993; Katsuura and Taha, 2014; Mucha and Iversen, 1986; Ward et al., 2006; Woolley et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 1998; Zhang and Kelley, 1997)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Activation of MORs in the NAc core by exogenous agonists increases consumption of a high-fat liquid in part by increasing the number of licking bouts.
source: Further supporting this idea, activation of MORs in the NAc core by exogenous agonists increases consumption of a high-fat liquid in part by increasing the number of licking bouts (perhaps as a result of increasing the number of approaches to the lickometer) (Katsuura et al., 2011; Lardeux et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Katsuura et al., 2011 and Lardeux et al., 2015

claim: Exogenous activation of NAc MORs promotes operant behavior for food reward.
source: Moreover, exogenous activation of NAc MORs promotes operant behavior for food reward (Zhang et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2003

claim: Exogenous activation of NAc MORs is sufficient to increase operant responses to cues predictive of high-calorie food in a Pavlovian-instrumental transfer (PIT) test.
source: and in fact is sufficient to increase operant responses to cues predictive of high-calorie food in a Pavlovian-instrumental transfer (PIT) test (Peciña and Berridge, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Peciña and Berridge, 2013

claim: Injection of CTAP into the NAc does not reduce consumption of a high-fat liquid in free fed rats.
source: Further arguing against an intermediate effect on consumption, we observed previously that injection of CTAP into the NAc does not reduce consumption of a high-fat liquid in free fed rats (Lardeux et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lardeux et al., 2015

claim: Excitations in a small population of NAc neurons encode the value of liquid rewards during consumption.
source: Indeed, excitations in a small population of NAc neurons encode the value of liquid rewards during consumption (Taha and Fields, 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Taha and Fields, 2005

claim: A large population of NAc neurons are inhibited in proportion to the rate of licking during consumption.
source: However, more likely contributors to consumption are the large population of NAc neurons that are inhibited in proportion to the rate of licking during consumption (Taha and Fields, 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Taha and Fields, 2005

claim: Experimental silencing of NAc neurons drives consumption.
source: Together with findings that experimental silencing of NAc neurons drives consumption (Reynolds and Berridge, 2001; Stratford and Kelley, 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to Reynolds and Berridge, 2001 and Stratford and Kelley, 1997

claim: Consumption is interrupted by brief excitation of the NAc.
source: whereas consumption is interrupted by brief excitation of the NAc (Krause et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Krause et al., 2010

claim: Generalized inhibition of the NAc results in nonspecific increases in food intake.
source: consistent with previous findings that generalized inhibition of the NAc results in nonspecific increases in food intake
evidence: Supported by reference to established findings

claim: MOR activation results in preferential increases in consumption of calorie-dense, and especially high-fat, food.
source: whereas MOR activation results in preferential increases in consumption of calorie-dense, and especially high-fat, food (Katsuura and Taha, 2014; Ward et al., 2006; Woolley et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 1998; Zhang and Kelley, 1997)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Activation of NAc MORs induces a preference for fat over carbohydrates.
source: The latter observation is consistent with previous studies indicating that activation of NAc MORs induces a preference for fat over carbohydrates (Taha, 2010; Zhang et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citations to Taha, 2010 and Zhang et al., 1998

claim: Activation of NAc MORs induces greater preference for the already-preferred flavor of two foods with equivalent nutritional content.
source: however, similar manipulations also induce greater preference for the already-preferred flavor of two foods with equivalent nutritional content (Woolley et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Woolley et al., 2006

claim: β-funaltrexamine (β-FNA) reduces rats' speed during runway approach to calorie-dense food.
source: One exception is the observation that β-funaltrexamine (β-FNA), a long-lasting MOR antagonist, reduces rats' speed during runway approach to calorie-dense food (Shin et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Shin et al., 2010

claim: NAc injection of β-FNA reduces spontaneous locomotion.
source: However, NAc injection of β-FNA has also been shown to reduce spontaneous locomotion (Kelley et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelley et al., 1996

claim: β-FNA reduces calorie-dense food consumption after NAc injection.
source: Such effects could potentially also explain the reduction in calorie-dense food consumption after β-FNA injection in the NAc (Bodnar et al., 1995; Kelley et al., 1996; Lenard et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: CTAP does not impair spontaneous locomotion when injected in the NAc.
source: Intriguingly, the MOR antagonist we used, CTAP, does not impair spontaneous locomotion when injected in the NAc (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: MOR antagonists can reduce food consumption after mild (<24 hr) restriction.
source: Although MOR antagonists can reduce food consumption after mild (<24 hr) restriction (Bodnar et al., 1995; Kelley et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bodnar et al., 1995 and Kelley et al., 1996

claim: Prominent populations of NAc neurons are excited and inhibited by cues that evoke approach behavior.
source: As observed previously (Ambroggi et al., 2011; du Hoffmann and Nicola, 2014; McGinty et al., 2013; Morrison et al., 2017; Nicola et al., 2004a), we found that prominent populations of NAc neurons are excited and inhibited by cues that evoke approach behavior (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: Changes in NAc neuronal firing begin prior to initiation of approach movement.
source: Previously, we established that these changes in firing begin prior to initiation of approach movement
evidence: Supported by reference to prior work by the authors

claim: The magnitude of NAc neuronal firing changes predicts the latency and speed of approach.
source: and that the magnitude of the firing changes predicts the latency and speed of approach (McGinty et al., 2013; Morrison et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to McGinty et al., 2013 and Morrison et al., 2017

claim: Cue-evoked excitations, but not inhibitions, are dopamine-dependent.
source: Cue-evoked excitations, but not inhibitions, are dopamine-dependent
evidence: Supported by reference to prior findings

claim: Injection of dopamine receptor antagonists reduces both cued approach and cue-evoked excitations.
source: because injection of dopamine receptor antagonists reduces both cued approach and cue-evoked excitations (du Hoffmann and Nicola, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to du Hoffmann and Nicola, 2014

claim: Exogenous activation of MORs can increase dopamine levels.
source: This idea is consistent with previous findings that exogenous activation of MORs can increase dopamine levels (Borg and Taylor, 1997; Hipólito et al., 2008; Hirose et al., 2005; Okutsu et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Dopamine release can be modulated at the terminal.
source: and with observations that dopamine release can be modulated at the terminal (Cachope and Cheer, 2014; Wenzel and Cheer, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cachope and Cheer, 2014 and Wenzel and Cheer, 2018

claim: Dopamine neurons are strongly regulated by the state of caloric need, with greater activation in higher need states.
source: Moreover, dopamine neurons are strongly regulated by the state of caloric need, with greater activation in higher need states (Meye and Adan, 2014; Nicola, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Meye and Adan, 2014 and Nicola, 2016

claim: Dopamine release evoked by food-predictive cues is greater in food-restricted rats than free-fed rats.
source: and in fact dopamine release evoked by food-predictive cues is greater in food-restricted rats than free-fed rats (Aitken et al., 2016; Cone et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Aitken et al., 2016 and Cone et al., 2014

claim: The endogenous ligand for NAc MORs is presumably enkephalin released by the large population of D2 receptor-expressing spiny neurons.
source: Presumably, the endogenous ligand for NAc MORs is enkephalin released by the large population of D2 receptor-expressing spiny neurons (Gerfen et al., 1990; Mansour et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerfen et al., 1990 and Mansour et al., 1995

claim: Opioids can be released somatodendritically and act as retrograde messengers.
source: alternatively, while it has not been demonstrated in the NAc, opioids can be released somatodendritically and act as a retrograde messengers (Iremonger and Bains, 2009; Wagner et al., 1993; Wamsteeker Cusulin et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Iremonger and Bains, 2009; Wagner et al., 1993; and Wamsteeker Cusulin et al., 2013

claim: In the dorsomedial striatum, enkephalin levels are elevated during meal onset.
source: however, in the dorsomedial striatum, enkephalin levels are elevated during meal onset (DiFeliceantonio et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to DiFeliceantonio et al., 2012

claim: MOR antagonists are currently used to treat obesity.
source: Although MOR antagonists are currently used to treat obesity (Apovian, 2016; Ziauddeen et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Apovian, 2016 and Ziauddeen et al., 2013

claim: Endogenous NAc opioids promote approach to high-fat food in the absence of caloric need.
source: Here, we test the hypothesis that endogenous NAc opioids also promote appetitive approach to calorie-dense food in states of relatively high satiety
evidence: This is the main hypothesis tested and supported by the experimental results

claim: NAc MOR activation is required for behavioral responding to reward-predictive cues in ad libitum chow-fed rats.
source: By simultaneously recording from NAc neurons and injecting a MOR antagonist into the NAc, we show that NAc MOR activation is required for both behavioral responding to reward-predictive cues and the neural encoding of those cues by NAc neurons. Importantly, these effects were observed in ad libitum chow-fed rats but not in those that had been food restricted
evidence: Supported by experimental results from simultaneous recording and pharmacology experiments

claim: NAc MOR activation is required for neural encoding of reward-predictive cues by NAc neurons in ad libitum chow-fed rats.
source: By simultaneously recording from NAc neurons and injecting a MOR antagonist into the NAc, we show that NAc MOR activation is required for both behavioral responding to reward-predictive cues and the neural encoding of those cues by NAc neurons. Importantly, these effects were observed in ad libitum chow-fed rats but not in those that had been food restricted
evidence: Supported by experimental results from simultaneous recording and pharmacology experiments

claim: Activation of NAc MORs promotes the approach to palatable food only in the absence of a homeostatic need for calories.
source: This striking dichotomy indicates that activation of NAc MORs promotes the approach to palatable food only in the absence of a homeostatic need for calories – i.e., hunger – suggesting that these receptors contribute to a neural mechanism that drives intake of calorie-dense food specifically in the state of satiety
evidence: Supported by the differential effects of CTAP in free-fed vs food-restricted rats

claim: NAc MORs contribute to a neural mechanism that drives intake of calorie-dense food specifically in the state of satiety.
source: This striking dichotomy indicates that activation of NAc MORs promotes the approach to palatable food only in the absence of a homeostatic need for calories – i.e., hunger – suggesting that these receptors contribute to a neural mechanism that drives intake of calorie-dense food specifically in the state of satiety
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing state-dependent effects of CTAP

claim: NAc core MORs act primarily to promote food seeking rather than consumption itself.
source: Thus, we conclude that NAc core MORs act primarily to promote food seeking rather than consumption itself
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including effects on cue-evoked firing and lack of effects on consumption-related firing

claim: NAc MORs specifically promote approach to high-fat foods.
source: Thus, our results suggest that NAc MORs specifically promote approach to high-fat foods
evidence: Supported by the differential effects of CTAP on cream vs sucrose reward

claim: This is the first report of a satiety state-dependent contribution of endogenous NAc opioids to food-seeking behavior.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of a satiety state-dependent contribution of endogenous NAc opioids to food-seeking behavior
evidence: Authors' assessment of the novelty of their findings
